topic: Explain how rain forms, for 8 year olds

slides.headline: Where does rain come from?
slides.body: The answer starts with the sun and a puddle.

slots.headline: Where does rain come from?
slots.body: The answer starts with the sun and a puddle.

slides.headline: The sun makes water disappear into the air.
slides.body: The sun warms up water in oceans, lakes, and even puddles. The water turns into an invisible gas called water vapor and rises up into the sky.

slots.headline: The sun makes water disappear into the air.
slots.body: The sun warms up water in oceans, lakes, and even puddles. The water turns into an invisible gas called water vapor and rises up into the sky.

slides.headline: Water vapor cools and makes tiny water droplets.
slides.body: High up in the sky, the air is very cold. The water vapor cools down and turns back into tiny liquid drops. These drops clump together to form clouds.

slots.headline: Water vapor cools and makes tiny water droplets.
slots.body: High up in the sky, the air is very cold. The water vapor cools down and turns back into tiny liquid drops. These drops clump together to form clouds.

slides.headline: When clouds get heavy, drops fall as rain.
slides.body: When the tiny droplets in a cloud become too heavy, they start to fall. If the air is warm, they fall as rain. If it is very cold, they fall as snow or hail.

slots.headline: When clouds get heavy, drops fall as rain.
slots.body: When the tiny droplets in a cloud become too heavy, they start to fall. If the air is warm, they fall as rain. If it is very cold, they fall as snow or hail.

slides.headline: Then it all starts over.
slides.body: The rain that falls flows into rivers, lakes, and oceans. The sun warms that water, turning it into vapor again. Up it goes to make new clouds and more rain. This never-ending loop is called the water cycle.

slots.headline: Then it all starts over.
slots.body: The rain that falls flows into rivers, lakes, and oceans. The sun warms that water, turning it into vapor again. Up it goes to make new clouds and more rain. This never-ending loop is called the water cycle.

slides.headline: You can spot the water cycle!
slides.body: You now know how rain forms. Watch the sky and understand what's happening.

slots.headline: You can spot the water cycle!

factCheckFindings: Slide 1 (body): "Investors don't want to see how big the market is. They want to see how you become valuable." distorts the facts (F5 says TAM slides are the most common source of credibility destruction, not that investors don't want to see market size at all. F9 says many founders can exp) → TAM slides are the most common source of credibility destruction in pitch decks. Focus on how you become valuable, not just market size.

Slide 2 (statLabel): "of startups fail due to running out of capital" distorts the facts (F1 says running out of capital is cited in 70% of cases per CB Insights, not that 70% of startups fail due to running out of capital. The label drops the qualif) → of startup failures cite running out of capital as a reason

Slide 5 (headline): "TAM slides are credibility killers" distorts the facts (F5 says TAM slides are the most common source of credibility destruction, not that they are 'credibility killers' which overstates the claim.) → TAM slides are the most common source of credibility destruction in pitch decks

Slide 5 (body): "TAM slides are the #1 credibility killer because they show market size, not market strategy." distorts the facts (F5 says TAM slides are the most common source of credibility destruction, but does not say the reason is because they show market size not market strategy. The ) → TAM slides are the most common source of credibility destruction in pitch decks. Focus on market strategy, not just size.

Slide 7 (body): "According to F12, clarity is the most important attribute of any pitch deck, but it is not a replacement for a meeting." distorts the facts (The slide cites 'F12' as if it's a source, but F12 is an internal fact ID, not a real source. The claim itself matches F12, but the citation is fabricated.) → Clarity is the most important attribute of any pitch deck; it is not a replacement for a meeting.

extra.hook: Your TAM slide is killing your credibility

judge.notes: The deck repeats the TAM slide point across slides 1 and 5, creating redundancy. The closing slide is too vague—'Audit your deck. Cut every slide that doesn't answer' lacks a concrete, actionable takeaway for founders.

factCheckFindings: Slide 1 (headline): "Using all your brain at once causes seizures" distorts the facts (F3 says 'would likely trigger an epileptic seizure', not 'causes seizures' as a general fact.) → Using all your brain at once would likely trigger an epileptic seizure.

Slide 2 (headline): "The 10% brain myth started in 1929" distorts the facts (F9 says the 1929 World Almanac stated the claim, but F12 says the precise origin remains unknown.) → The 10% brain myth was stated in the 1929 World Almanac, but its precise origin remains unknown.

Slide 5 (listItems): "William James: People use only a fraction of their mental potential." distorts the facts (F8 says William James told lecture audiences that people only meet a fraction of their full mental potential, not 'use only a fraction'.) → William James: People only meet a fraction of their full mental potential.

extra.hook: Using all your brain at once causes seizures

judge.notes: Two biggest problems: (1) Slide 1 and Slide 4 incorrectly claim that using all brain at once triggers seizures, which is not a standard neuroscientific finding and misrepresents the debunking; (2) Slide 2 cites a 1929 almanac as the origin but the myth predates that, and the stat number is misleadingly presented as fact.

factCheckFindings: Slide 1 (body): "Knowledge workers face 275 daily interruptions, each costing 23 minutes to regain focus. That's over 100 hours lost annually." distorts the facts (F10 states 275 interruptions per day and 23 minutes 15 seconds to regain focus, but the 100 hours lost is a calculation not in FACTS and the phrasing implies ea) → Knowledge workers face 275 interruptions per day, and it takes an average of 23 minutes and 15 seconds to regain deep focus after a single disruption.

Slide 2 (body): "Each of 275 daily interruptions costs 23 minutes and 15 seconds to regain focus. That's over 100 hours of lost deep work yearly." distorts the facts (F10 gives the interruption count and recovery time, but the 100 hours lost is not in FACTS and the claim implies each interruption causes that full loss, which ) → Knowledge workers face 275 interruptions per day, and it takes an average of 23 minutes and 15 seconds to regain deep focus after a single disruption.

Slide 3 (splitLeft): "In the office: 2 hours 48 minutes of productive work per 8-hour day." distorts the facts (F9 states 'average knowledge worker gets 2 hours 48 minutes of productive work per 8-hour office day', but the slide's 'productive work' is not specified as 'de) → The average knowledge worker gets 2 hours 48 minutes of productive work per 8-hour office day.

Slide 3 (splitRight): "Remote: 3 hours 36 minutes of deep focus — a 29% gain." distorts the facts (F9 states 'remote workers average 3 hours 36 minutes of deep focus work', but the 29% gain is a calculation not in FACTS and the comparison mixes 'productive wo) → Remote workers average 3 hours 36 minutes of deep focus work.

Slide 4 (listItems): "Gen X: 68% report higher productivity when remote." distorts the facts (F6 states 'Gen X is the biggest beneficiary of remote work productivity, with 68% reporting higher productivity', but the slide omits the qualifier 'reporting h) → Gen X: 68% report higher productivity when remote (F6).

Slide 4 (listItems): "Women: 66% say remote boosted output vs 59% of men." distorts the facts (F7 states 'Women are more likely than men to say remote work has boosted their output (66% versus 59%)', but the slide changes 'boosted their output' to 'remote) → Women: 66% say remote work has boosted their output, versus 59% of men.

Slide 4 (listItems): "Software developers: 35% more code commits daily when remote." distorts the facts (F8 states 'Software developers working remotely produce 35% more code commits per day than those in open-plan offices', but the slide drops the comparison group) → Software developers: 35% more code commits per day when remote than those in open-plan offices.

Slide 6 (body): "71% of senior leaders call meetings unproductive. Remote work shifts time from meetings to deep work tools, now 51% of work time. Communication and meetings tak" distorts the facts (F11 states '71% of senior leaders describe meetings as unproductive or inefficient', but the slide says 'call meetings unproductive' which drops 'or inefficient) → 71% of senior leaders describe meetings as unproductive or inefficient. 51% of work time is spent in deep work tools, 34% in communication tools, and 15% in meetings.

extra.hook: What if interruptions cost you 100 hours of deep work per year?

judge.notes: Two biggest problems: (1) Accuracy is low because the deck uses invented or unverifiable statistics (e.g., '275 interruptions per day,' '106 hours yearly,' '23 minutes 15 seconds' are not standard or cited; the '35% more code commits' and '68% of Gen X' lack sources). (2) Flow suffers from repetition: slides 1 and 2 both focus on interruption cost and the same 23-minute stat, making the argument feel redundant rather than building.

topic: A 12 slide deep dive on how transformer models work

slides.headline: DeBERTa surpassed human performance on SuperGLUE
slides.body: Transformer models scale from millions to trillions of parameters using attention, feed-forward layers, and embeddings.

slots.headline: DeBERTa surpassed human performance on SuperGLUE
slots.body: Transformer models scale from millions to trillions of parameters using attention, feed-forward layers, and embeddings.

slides.headline: Transformers process all tokens simultaneously
slides.body: Unlike RNNs, transformers don't process tokens one by one. Instead, self-attention computes weighted connections between every token pair in a single forward pass, enabling parallel computation and capturing long-range dependencies.

slots.headline: Transformers process all tokens simultaneously
slots.body: Unlike RNNs, transformers don't process tokens one by one. Instead, self-attention computes weighted connections between every token pair in a single forward pass, enabling parallel computation and capturing long-range dependencies.

slides.headline: Each token becomes a dense vector
slides.body: The first step maps each input token to a dense vector of fixed size, typically 768 dimensions. This embedding table has dimensions vocab_size × embedding_dim. For example, a model with vocab 50,257 and dim 768 had a total of 77 million parameters.

slots.headline: Each token becomes a dense vector

slides.headline: Attention weighs token relationships in parallel
slides.body: For each token, the mechanism computes query, key, and value vectors. The attention score is the scaled dot-product of query and key vectors, determining how much to mix values.

slots.headline: Attention weighs token relationships in parallel

slides.headline: Feed-forward networks add non-linearity
slides.body: After attention, each token's vector passes through a two-layer perceptron: an expansion to a larger hidden dimension, a ReLU activation, then a projection back. This adds depth and capacity for learning complex patterns.

slots.headline: Feed-forward networks add non-linearity
slots.body: After attention, each token's vector passes through a two-layer perceptron: an expansion to a larger hidden dimension, a ReLU activation, then a projection back. This adds depth and capacity for learning complex patterns.

slides.headline: Transformers stack dozens of identical blocks
slides.body: Each block contains one self-attention sublayer and one feed-forward sublayer. Residual connections bypass each sublayer, adding input to output. Layer normalization stabilizes training, enabling very deep networks without vanishing gradients.

factCheckFindings: Slide 3 (body): "This embedding table has dimensions vocab_size × embedding_dim, and in one simplified model (vocab 50,257, dim 768) it accounts for 77 million parameters." distorts the facts (F4 states the model had 77 million parameters total, not just the embedding table.) → This embedding table has dimensions vocab_size × embedding_dim, and in one simplified model (vocab 50,257, dim 768) it contributed to a total of 77 million parameters.

Slide 10 (body): "Phi 4 (10B–50B) scores 84.8% on MMLU, while Llama 3.3 70B (50B–100B) scores 86.3%—a 1.5% improvement for 20 billion more parameters." distorts the facts (F10 says Llama 3.3 70B shows a marginal climb to 86.3% on MMLU, a 1.5% gain over Phi 4. The slide implies 20B extra parameters caused the gain, but F11 says pay) → Phi 4 (10B–50B) scores 84.8% on MMLU, while Llama 3.3 70B (50B–100B) scores 86.3%—a 1.5% gain over Phi 4.

Slide 11 (body): "Microsoft DeBERTa surpassed human performance on SuperGLUE for the first time, scoring 89.9 vs. 89.8." distorts the facts (F12 says DeBERTa surpassed human performance for the first time with a macro-average score of 89.9 versus 89.8. The slide omits 'macro-average' which is a speci) → Microsoft DeBERTa surpassed human performance on the SuperGLUE benchmark for the first time with a macro-average score of 89.9 versus 89.8.

extra.hook: DeBERTa surpassed human performance on SuperGLUE

judge.notes: The deck fails to meet the requirement of explaining how transformer models work for developers new to ML. It deviates into parameter count and benchmark comparisons (slides 7-11), which are not part of the requested deep dive. The hero slide uses DeBERTa as a headline, which is confusing and not a clear hook for the intended audience. The logical flow is broken after slide 6, and the closing slide is too vague.
